title: Pandarus killed; Aeneas struck down
intro: Athena guides Diomedes’ answering spear. Aeneas bravely defends the fallen Pandarus, only to be disabled by a stone. The page ends at the point where a normal death narrative is interrupted by divine rescue.

notes.text: Diomedes predicts that they will not stop ‘before one of you, fallen, has sated Ares with blood.’ ἆσαι is aorist active infinitive of ἄω, ‘sate’; αἵματος is the genitive of what fills him. πεσόντα is aorist participle of πίπτω. ταλαύρινος characterizes Ares as a tough warrior, conventionally ‘shield-bearing / enduring under the shield.’

προέηκε is epic aorist of προΐημι, ‘sent forth.’ ἴθυνεν, from ἰθύνω, means ‘directed straight,’ with Athena explicitly the subject. ῥῖνα is accusative singular of ῥίς, ‘nose’; παρά with ὀφθαλμόν locates the entry beside the eye. ἐπέρησεν is aorist of περάω, ‘passed through / pierced.’

πρυμνήν describes the tongue at its root. τάμε is unaugmented second aorist of τέμνω; χαλκός is subject, the weapon named by its metal. ἀτειρής means ‘unyielding, indestructible.’ ἀνθερεών is the chin, with νείατον, ‘lowest.’ ἐξελύθη, aorist passive of ἐκλύω, describes the point emerging free below it.

αἰόλος conveys shifting, glittering appearance; παμφανόωντα is an epic expanded participle meaning ‘flashing brightly,’ both agreeing with τεύχεα. παρέτρεσσαν is aorist of παρατρέω, ‘shied aside,’ describing the horses’ reaction. λύθη is unaugmented aorist passive of λύω; ψυχή and μένος leave the dying man as his bodily strength collapses.

δείσας is aorist participle of δείδω, ‘fearing.’ ἐρυσαίατο is epic third-plural aorist middle optative of ἐρύω, ‘drag away,’ after the past-tense context of fear. The object is νεκρόν, Pandarus’ corpse. οἱ marks Aeneas’ personal interest: the body must not be taken from him.

βαῖνε is unaugmented imperfect of βαίνω, describing his defensive stance or movement around the body. πεποιθώς is perfect active participle of πείθω with intransitive meaning ‘trusting,’ taking dative ἀλκί, ‘strength / courage.’ κτάμεναι is an epic aorist infinitive of κτείνω after μεμαώς. ὅς τις … ἔλθοι is a generalizing relative clause, ‘whoever should approach.’

σμερδαλέα is adverbial, ‘terribly,’ with Aeneas’ shout. The subject then switches to Diomedes, named on the next line. χερμάδιον is a hand-thrown stone, here of enormous size. φέροιεν is potential optative: two present-day men could not carry it. The narrator contrasts the heroic past with the diminished strength of contemporary mortals.

ἄνδρε is nominative dual, but φέροιεν is plural, another ordinary Homeric mixture. ῥέα means ‘easily’; οἶος here is ‘alone,’ not the relative οἷος, ‘such as.’ μέγα ἔργον describes the stone as a formidable task or burden. Diomedes’ easy handling makes the discrepancy in strength visible.

ἰσχίον is the hip; μηρός the thigh. κοτύλη, literally a hollow cup, names the hip socket. ἐνστρέφεται is present middle/passive of ἐνστρέφω, describing the joint’s normal movement. θλάσσε is aorist of θλάω, ‘crushed’; ῥῆξε is aorist of ῥήγνυμι, ‘tore.’ τένοντε is accusative dual, the two tendons.

ῥινός here means ‘skin,’ unlike ῥίς, ‘nose,’ earlier on the page. ὦσε … ἀπό means the rough stone pushed or tore the skin away. γνύξ, ‘on the knees,’ accompanies ἐριπών from ἐρείπω, ‘fall.’ ἐρείσατο is aorist middle of ἐρείδω, ‘braced himself,’ with instrumental χειρί and genitive γαίης, the surface against which he supports himself.

notes.lemma: καί νύ κεν … ἀπόλοιτο, εἰ μή
notes.text: A vivid unreal rescue formula: ‘and now Aeneas would have perished, had Aphrodite not noticed.’ ἀπόλοιτο is aorist middle optative of ἀπόλλυμι, used with κεν for the unreal outcome, although the rescuing condition has indicative νόησε. τέκε is unaugmented aorist of τίκτω; βουκολέοντι describes Anchises tending cattle when Aphrodite conceived Aeneas by him.
